channel.title: Tangle - the good parts
channel.description: Tangle's daily edition cut down to Today's topic (the story, what the left and right are saying, and Isaac Saul's take) and Under the radar, plus Isaac's standalone essays. Sponsors, quick hits, extras, teasers, paywalled previews and the Sunday recap are left out.

item.title: The U.S. loses measles elimination status.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, the latest on a new education-funding program.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

Measles. On Tuesday, November 17, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced that the United States has lost its measles elimination status. The loss of status follows 12 months of sustained domestic transmission of the disease. 

Back up: The U.S. gained measles elimination status in 2000 and maintained the designation until this year. In 2025, a series of outbreaks began in communities across the country, predominantly among people who were not vaccinated against the disease. Globally, measles outbreaks have increased in many countries, also in concert with declining vaccination rates. Mexico lost its elimination status on November 17, and Canada lost its elimination status in November 2025.

As of November 19, 5,838 confirmed measles cases have been reported in the U.S. in 2026, with 43 new outbreaks (compared to 48 total in 2025 and 16 in 2024). According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 11% of those cases have resulted in hospitalizations, and six people have died from measles-related causes. Weekly cases began rising in July, and the week of November 1 had a year-high 351 reported cases. 

Following PAHO’s announcement, CDC Director Erica Schwartz said in a statement, “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does… We remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” In a post on X, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said, “We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”

Today, we’ll share views from the right, left, and health professionals on the measles outbreaks. Then, Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right criticize Secretary Kennedy’s role in the outbreaks.
  • Others say distrust of the medical establishment is causing vaccination rates to drop.

The Wall Street Journal editorial board argued “official vaccine skepticism has aided [measles’s] comeback.”

“Most outbreaks have occurred in pockets with low vaccination rates such as rural areas of Texas, South Carolina, Pennsylvania and Utah. About 95% or so of people in a community need to be inoculated to protect those who can’t be vaccinated, such as infants, and vaccinated individuals with weak immune systems,” the board said. “Covid vaccine mandates and deceptions by public health officials spurred skepticism of decades-old vaccines.”

“Mr. Kennedy has also given credence to the falsehood that the MMR vaccine causes autism despite dozens of studies to the contrary,” the board wrote. “The HHS Secretary no doubt views increasing skepticism of vaccines as a success, even if the result is more measles. His acolytes say he’s not to blame for America’s measles resurgence since other countries like the U.K. and Canada have also lost measles elimination status. But those countries have vaccine access challenges caused by their socialized health systems.”

In PJ Media, Athena Thorne wrote “the left rushes to convict MAHA [over measles]. Not so fast.”

“Undercutting the predictable leftist attempt to use this development as anti-Trump fodder is the fact that, among the developed nations, the United States is late to the game in losing its measles-free status,” Thorne said. “Just over a year ago, on Nov. 10, 2025, PAHO yanked the accolade from Canada. And then, at the very beginning of this year, WHO announced it had decided to strip several European nations of their status in September 2025, based on data from the previous year.”

“Clearly, RFK didn’t jet-set from nation to nation, scaring people away from vaccinating their kids against measles… So if RFK isn’t to blame for dropping vaccination rates, who is?” Thorne asked. “The answer is that Big Medicine did this to itself. As much as the left wants to try to gin up the situation into a CRISIS!™ with which to unseat RFK and the MAHA movement, the fact is that Kennedy’s ascendancy is a symptom of Big Pharma’s malady, not the cause.”

What the left is saying.
  • The left is alarmed by the loss of the elimination status, suggesting it will have far-reaching consequences. 
  • Some blame Kennedy’s vaccine skepticism for exacerbating the problem.

In The Washington Post, Leana S. Wen wrote about “why it matters that the U.S. lost its measles-elimination status.”

“The loss [of the status] is more than a symbolic setback. It reflects a devastating reversal in public health progress with real consequences for Americans’ lives,” Wen said. “Pregnant women are at especially high risk of measles complications… At least 13 newborns were diagnosed with congenital measles, which can cause brain inflammation, serious neurological complications and death.”

“The consequences will go beyond the direct effects on health. Measles has an incubation period of up to 21 days, and unvaccinated people exposed to the virus may be required to quarantine for that period. That could result in weeks of missed school and work,” Wen wrote. “Not long ago, the U.S. took great pride in being a leader in global health. It’s hard to maintain that moral authority when it can no longer control a vaccine-preventable disease within its borders.”

In Bloomberg, Lisa Jarvis called the loss of elimination status “America’s shame.”

“Measles cases started flaring up in Texas around the same time that Kennedy was confirmed, meaning he didn’t start that fire. But at nearly every opportunity, he fanned the flames,” Jarvis said. “That included pushing junk science and fake cures, and spending months equivocating over the value of the measles, mumps and rubella shot. (Eventually, he did say that the MMR vaccine offers the best protection against the virus.)

“What followed was even worse: devastating cuts at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, an overhaul of the agency’s influential vaccine advisory committee to appoint vaccine skeptics, and a suite of policies seemingly crafted to further erode Americans’ confidence in and access to early childhood vaccines,” Jarvis wrote. “What should scare us most is that the return of widespread measles could be just the start as Kennedy’s influence over Americans’ health grows.”

What health professionals are saying.
  • Some health professionals say that regaining elimination status starts at the local level.
  • Others say Congress has a key role in the effort.

In MedPage Today, Drs. Barbara Rubino, S. Monica Soni, Priya Shete, and Erica Pan suggested “how to get [elimination status] back.”

“The first step is to make it easy and affordable for children to get the MMR vaccine,” the authors said. “[But] getting the MMR vaccine may not be as simple as scheduling a visit with the pediatrician. The portion of children with a ‘usual source of care,’ like a trusted pediatrician or health clinic, has been declining since 2014; more than 30% of children lack age-appropriate preventive care visits each year.”

“Public health, clinic systems, and community-based organizations must make it easier to access immunization by bringing vaccines to where people live and spend time. Places like local pharmacies, health fairs, schools, and community centers should be prioritized for funding and resources,” the authors said. “To increase the number of pharmacies available as vaccine access points, health department partnerships with state pharmacy boards and pharmacy chains are critical. Policies that expand pharmacists’ ability to vaccinate young children can improve access too.”

In STAT, Dr. Krutika Kuppalli argued “Congress must demand resources to fight measles on the local level.”

“In its first funding bills, the new Congress should protect the Vaccines for Children program and provide multiyear funding for health departments to work with schools and pediatric practices in communities with the lowest vaccination coverage,” Kuppalli wrote. “It should pay for staff who can call families whose children are overdue, answer questions about vaccine side effects, help them find immunization records, and offer appointments after school or on Saturdays.”

“Congress should also ask the CDC to report publicly each quarter on whether two-dose MMR coverage is rising in the communities with the largest gaps and if it is not increasing, to explain what the challenges are to vaccination,” Kuppalli said. “These reports would help Congress understand where more help is needed and build the record the U.S. needs to demonstrate at least 12 months without sustained measles transmission.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • It’s easy to blame the Trump administration for the loss of status, but measles’ resurgence is a more complicated story.
  • Both vaccine skepticism and the medical establishment’s actions bear responsibility.
  • The only way to reverse the trend is to increase vaccination rates.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

It’s tempting to embrace the simplest version of this story:

President Trump nominated Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a vaccine skeptic, to be Health secretary. Kennedy was confirmed, then announced publicly (and repeatedly insisted) that he’d investigate all manner of vaccine injury, including the claim that they cause autism. Then measles vaccination rates dropped, cases surged, and we lost our measles elimination status.

Simple. But also terribly incomplete.

For one, measles cases began ticking back up in the United States before Kennedy was even confirmed. I remember this vividly, because about a year and a half ago I was flying to Texas with my eight-week-old son in the middle of a measles outbreak in the state. My flight was in mid-March. Kennedy had been confirmed in February. The outbreak had been going on for months. I consulted some epidemiologists about how to mitigate risk and ended up changing my flight from the Midland-Odessa airport to El Paso to put some miles between us and the heart of the outbreak. 

Second, as Athena Thorne noted (under “What the right is saying”), Canada lost its measles-free status in November of 2025 from an outbreak that began in October 2024. Then Britain and several other European countries lost their status in January of 2026 based on epidemiological data from 2024. In fact, in 13 countries, including France, Germany and Italy, measles is now considered endemic. The world has been facing fresh threats from this virus since before Kennedy began influencing health policy.

In fact, the measles outbreak that ended our elimination status may have started in Canada before spreading to Texas and northern Mexico in early 2025. Mexican and U.S. officials have confirmed matching genetic strains; it’s the same outbreak.

Which is all just to say: Let’s not overstate or oversimplify Kennedy’s role.

At the same time, though, the Health secretary’s job — and the federal government’s — is to prevent these outbreaks from worsening. And we know how to stop measles: vaccines. So it’s clear that dropping rates of vaccination, or increased skepticism about the vaccines, would cause more measles outbreaks. That part of the story is not all that complicated. 

But Canada losing its status in the same outbreak is also an indictment of our response; it means we failed to anticipate the virus, and that we were just as unprepared as Canada and Mexico (maybe more so). Now, we’re paying the price. The confirmed U.S. case count, above 5,000, is the largest outbreak we’ve had since 1991. That’s a knock against the outgoing Biden administration, which was in charge as vaccine rates fell, and a knock against the current Trump administration, which has overseen our response to the entirety of this outbreak. It’s also a knock against anyone who sows doubt about the MMR vaccine, particularly anyone as prominent as Secretary Kennedy.

Kennedy’s role in sowing doubt and confusion about vaccines predates his time as Health secretary. Kennedy has repeatedly joined anti-vaccine advocates in claiming that childhood vaccines were the cause of rising rates of autism. In his 2023 book Vax-Unvax: Let the Science Speak, he defended Andrew Wakefield, the doctor whose retracted 1998 study started the still-ongoing MMR-autism scare. 

As recently as August, President Trump signed an executive order calling for breaking up the MMR vaccine schedule into single-disease shots. Trump argued that the combination of vaccines is “quite lethal” and breaking them up would “have a huge impact on autism.” Kennedy defended those claims, saying that the MMR vaccine was effective against measles but there wasn’t enough evidence on its safety (notably, a few weeks before these comments, a large-scale study in the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal found no association between the MMR vaccine and autism diagnoses). Concurrent with Kennedy’s prominent activism around vaccine safety has been a drop in trust or understanding of vaccines. 

Now that the outbreak is worsening, Kennedy is singing a noticeably more straightforward tune. Here is his statement from last week; see if you notice the difference: “We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”

And, again, while Kennedy himself is one prominent purveyor of vaccine skepticism, he’s hardly the lone cause of the movement’s popularity. The medical establishment also bears some responsibility. It did serious damage to its reputation before the pandemic, in large part due to the medical establishment merging with corporate interests. Many of us watched as opioids, which drug companies, doctors and federal regulators initially told us carried little risk of addiction, ravaged our communities. Elsewhere, we found out that the sugar industry had funded decades of dietary advice. Big Pharma ingratiated itself as a primary congressional lobbyist and even drafted the laws meant to regulate its own actions. All the while, price gouging and cost issues in the health care industry create an adversarial relationship between patients, health insurance companies, and doctors. 

And then the pandemic happened. 

Today, it’s easy to read a CDC statement or a government-funded study with skepticism; it’s even easier to believe that the people on TV telling you to vaccinate your kids don’t actually have their best interests in mind, especially when somewhere, somebody makes billions of dollars selling that vaccine. I feel that impulse all the time.

In truth, many Americans have become jaded and blind to the magic of our own medical achievements. I once spent a week in India observing the country’s effort to defeat polio. Overcrowded trains would pull into busy stations, and citizens would literally hang their babies out the windows of the train so doctors could administer vaccine drops into the baby’s mouth before the train pulled away — all in an effort to end this disease that was still ravaging communities in the 21st century. The people of India did it willingly, because they believed in the miracle of vaccines. They trusted their doctors (and their government). They were convinced through years of efforts to overcome skepticism and resistance. Then they saw the results. For the United States, there’s a lesson here: People can be won over through trust-building efforts, and mandates don’t solve everything.

And as bad as the recent numbers are, I suspect things may get worse. According to the CDC, vaccine exemptions among American kindergartners rose nearly 17% in just the past year, reaching a record 4.2%. And nearly 280,000 kindergartners attended school without documentation of completing the two-dose MMR vaccine. That’s potentially millions of children over the next decade, even if vaccination rates don't fall any further. And they're already falling. Canada’s population is smaller than ours, but according to epidemiologist Dr. Michael Osterholm, it has a similar epidemiological makeup. The country’s rate of infection, about a year ahead of where we are, would equal about 50,000 cases here. Something in that ballpark is probably our future, and that’s assuming we handle the outbreak roughly the same as Canada.

Increasing vaccination rates is the only way to reverse this trend. That rebound will start in one of two ways. One, the situation gets worse fast, and vaccination rates spike when everyone remembers what it’s like not to be protected against measles. Or two, the public health space does a good enough job communicating the necessity of the vaccine to restore trust before the situation devolves much further. That requires more than just Secretary Kennedy affirming his unambiguous endorsements of the vaccine. It requires selling how miraculous this technology is again. It requires convincing public health communication that reaches people who most need to hear it. 

I’ve got little confidence the country — or this administration — is capable of option two. So I’ll be bracing for the former while praying for the latter.

Take the survey: Will the U.S. regain measles elimination status? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The tech fragility is here.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: A string of outages has me reevaluating my previous writing.
item.content:encoded:
Back in April, Anthropic announced a new AI model called “Mythos” and said it was too dangerous to be released to the public. 

The company’s general message was: We built a product that’s so good at finding security vulnerabilities that we can’t release it publicly right now. Instead, we’ll launch a project (named Glasswing) to give American businesses a head start to shore up their security vulnerabilities before the public gets access to these tools. Anthropic said it expected other models to catch up in the coming months, at which point we’d see a slew of new tech vulnerabilities and cyber intrusions pop up across the world.

I saw this story through a simple lens: Anthropic was like a company selling a security system while telling you it had just identified all these fresh ways a burglar could break into your home. It was fear-mongering. Before, I’d been skeptical of these companies’ claims about their products; now, I was outright scornful. It felt like a marketing ploy from a bunch of people who were getting very good at talking about how powerful and advanced their product was.

I also wrote this:

If, over the next few months, everyone from Amazon to Chase to Meta starts scrambling to prepare for a new security threat, that will confirm to me that this threat is real. If these guys all play with the model and nothing really changes, I’ll assume that the threat was overhyped.

Well, it’s now been a few months. I pride myself on being an open-minded person willing to admit when I’m wrong and change my mind when presented with new evidence. Today, I have to admit: The threat is beginning to look very, very real. So it’s time for me to eat some crow and update my assessment. 

Based on our knowledge right now, the wave of outages, tech issues, and general all-encompassing tech fragility across various sectors is not the result of rogue AI bots. It isn’t cybercriminals, and it’s not Iran or China, either. It appears to be exactly what Anthropic said would happen. A bunch of large corporations, institutions, and tech companies are using rapidly developing AI tools to identify their own security issues. Then they are trying to update, patch, and fix those issues. And in many cases, they are breaking things along the way.

That’s really it. That’s the story: AI-assisted corporations and institutions are in a race against AI-assisted threats, and everyone is moving so fast that our already fragile systems are beginning to crack. 

Get more of the story...
We broke down the outages with just the facts, and then we picked out the best arguments from conservative, progressive, and independent writers in today's free newsletter so you can make up your own mind. Read them here. 

It isn’t your imagination that this is happening more frequently, either. Yes, part of it is that we are just noticing these failures — and this tech fragility — more. But we are also actually experiencing a higher frequency of outages. Rohit Krishnan, a Wharton fellow and author of Building God: Demystifying AI for Decision Makers, put together a helpful chart mapping rates of tech outages from the last 10 years. It shows we are not at all-time highs, but we are in a period of much higher system failures than normal. According to Krishnan, we haven’t seen this volume of disruptions across sectors since 2013. 

All of this has me seriously reconsidering my rather blasé attitude about the rapid development of AI. Among other things, in recent writings, I’ve said that on a scale of 1 to 10, with 1 being the very early stages of AI capabilities and 10 being AI as a fully realized technology, I think we are closer to a 7 than a 3. In other words, these models weren’t going to get much better than they are now. 

That thesis is looking less likely every day. The models and products are continuing to improve rapidly, and we are not getting many signals that they are slowing down. Mythos was just one marker on the highway, but Anthropic's warnings about what models like it would do appear to be accurate. 

I’ve also been skeptical about how dangerous it would be to allow these products to hit the open market. But a collection of events has changed my opinion there, too: I’ve had several conversations with friends, readers, and experts in the space who convinced me I should be more worried than I am. I listened to Bill Gates’s recent interview with Ezra Klein, which genuinely scared me, not least because Gates himself seemed so thoroughly afraid. The Google Threat Intelligence Group then warned this week that the “era of autonomous attacks has arrived,” and we are now up against a “hacker that doesn’t eat, sleep, or get tired, and never stops searching for a way in.” And through all of this, I’ve been watching news story after news story about all the ways major industries seem unprepared for this moment. 

Think about it this way: The FAA called a national ground stop, the NSA had an internal communication system crash, and online banking service issues popped up all in just the last week. Each was (purportedly) caused by attempts to update or patch vulnerable systems. Which has me thinking: If the people trying to be helpful can so easily break the things they are working to improve, what does that say about the odds that actual AI-assisted cyber criminals (or, God forbid, rogue AI agents) will have much trouble bringing all these institutions to their knees?

Given all this, I feel much less confident about our potential to prevent a banking collapse, rogue AI from escaping containment, or government systems from being compromised. All of a sudden, a multi-week grid collapse or the potential for the U.S. military to be kneecapped in a “cyber incident” doesn’t seem so far-fetched. It’s honestly starting to feel a little Pollyannaish to think it won’t happen.

There’s no “but” here. I’m frustrated and a little uneasy to say that I don’t have an optimistic landing. I take solace in people like John Hultquist, the chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, who said this week, “Things are going to go offline periodically as the world manages a generation of tech debt. It will be a nuisance, but it will be okay.” I hope it’s as simple as that, but I can’t say I share his optimism anymore.

The people leading the AI revolution seem hellbent on pushing forward no matter the cost, despite their constant warnings that they might wipe out all of humanity. The government leaders responsible for regulating away the dangers of these kinds of technologies are busy obsessing over what we call them, or are totally in cahoots with the AI leaders themselves, or are so technically illiterate that any attempt to be helpful is nearly useless. And the rest of us common folk are just along for the ride.

So here’s to hoping the techies, nerds, and their billionaire bosses know what they’re doing. Because it’s starting to feel like the game is afoot. And I can’t say I’m keen to find out who wins.

Staff dissent — Senior Editor Will Kaback: Assuming that most of the recent disruptions are a byproduct of companies and government agencies trying to patch vulnerabilities identified by new AI models, I have a different reaction than Isaac.

He writes, “If the people trying to be helpful can so easily break the things they are working to improve, what does that say about the odds that actual AI-assisted cyber criminals (or, God forbid, rogue AI agents) will have much trouble bringing all these institutions to their knees?” I would be far more alarmed if this work wasn’t being done — that is, it’s relatively reassuring that new vulnerabilities are being found and urgent work is being done to address them. That things are breaking along the way isn’t ideal, obviously, but I think it’s a reasonable price to pay to improve critical systems. I don’t see it as evidence that we’re on the precipice of mass cyberattacks.

I appreciate Isaac’s message about keeping an open mind on new developments, and I want to do the same. If the disruptions and outages become more significant — a major bank going down for multiple days, issues with the electrical grid, another ground stop that persists for more than a few hours — I’ll start to see the trade-offs differently. Just today, the European Commission said it was targeted by an “AI-generated cybercampaign,” and that’s cause for real concern. Similarly, if AI-enabled cyberattacks become more frequent and impactful despite the work being done to prevent them, I think it will mean Isaac’s theory is, distressingly, coming true.

For now, though, I’m viewing the underlying work behind the recent system outages more optimistically.

Moved by the take? Share it!

item.title: The tech outages.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, the things we didn’t cover this week.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The technology outages. Over the past week, a slew of outages across industries, service providers, and government agencies have heightened concerns about vulnerabilities in U.S. technology systems and the threat of artificial intelligence-driven cyberattacks. The notable examples include:

  • A multi-day global outage of Microsoft’s Outlook service, which the company said was caused in part by a “latent defect” in its systems
  • The Federal Aviation Administration calling a nationwide ground stop for most flights due to communications issues between planes and air traffic controllers
  • United Airlines delaying flight departures for several hours due to a temporary system outage
  • An outage of a classified network used by the National Security Agency for internal communications
  • A software issue affecting JPMorgan Chase’s online banking system
  • An interruption to human resources management company Workday’s services
  • An outage to Apple services, including the App Store, Apple Pay, and iCloud
  • A cyberattack on 178 websites — including Zoom, CNN, Salesforce, and Ikea — that attempted to steal cryptocurrency and hack iPhones

Aside from the attempts to hack the 178 websites, affected companies and the federal government have maintained that the issues were not cyberattacks or connected to one another. However, some experts have said to expect more outages in the near future as companies seek to patch vulnerabilities in their technology in response to AI-related threats. On Monday, the Google Threat Intelligence Group released a statement saying “the era of autonomous attacks has arrived,” adding, “Bad actors are now using autonomous LLM frameworks to continuously scan software updates, figure out what flaw was patched, and build an attack for it — all without human involvement.”

The Trump administration says the outages are not linked. “We have no indication that these incidents are related, that they’re coordinated,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said. “We also have no indication that they’re [the] result of a state-sponsored malign actor.” Furthermore, during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on Wednesday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, “I’m 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems.”

Below are views from the left and right on the outages, followed by Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • Many on the left say assessing the extent of the risk requires more information.  
  • Some argue the outages reveal weaknesses in America’s economic system.
  • Others suggest the Trump administration is not equipped to respond effectively.

In The Atlantic, Ian Bogost suggested the “incidents could be related — unless they are not.”

“The proximity of these events makes them feel related. And maybe they are, in a way,” Bogost wrote. “Computer systems of all kinds have always gone down briefly. It happens every day. Why, suddenly, are people pretending that they expect every one of these machines to always work properly? Seeking, finding, decoding, and interpreting information that would answer these questions proves difficult.” 

“The ignorance I am earnestly expressing about the nature of these events might later be proved foolhardy if a more widespread underlying circumstance reveals itself to be responsible, or even contributory,” Bogost said. “It would be both irresponsible to claim that I hold greater knowledge than the none that I actually possess, and embarrassing, besides, to be proved wrong. And so the door to a Widespread Problem must remain open to the unknowable future.”

In The Nation, Elie Mystal said “make America function again!”

“The United States is not failed, but it’s far from functional,” Mystal wrote. “Republicans run for office on the claim that government cannot work, and then spend their time in power destroying government just to prove that they were right. Neoliberals help Republicans by ceding critical government functions to the private sector, which in turn ignores the public good in an all-consuming chase for greater margins and profits.” 

“The problem is not that we’re reliant on technology; humans have always relied on technology… The problem is that the tech is no longer made to be reliable. The tech is made to make money,” Mystal said. “[AI] is a technology that few people understand, and worse, the ones who do understand it are warning us that they can’t control it. We’re also using the AI to replace human workers, so when the AI breaks, our only choice is to ask the AI how to fix it.”

In CNN, Stephen Collinson wrote about “what should really scare Americans.”

“There’s no public evidence that any of the recent incidents were due to cyberattacks by a hostile power or criminal organization,” Collinson said. “Fears over whether this string of meltdowns might be the work of some unknown adversary, while understandable, may be a distraction from more material questions. The past five days have raised vulnerabilities that speak to a disorienting moment in a transition to a volatile and potentially dangerous new technological era.” 

“Explaining how he’d fix the air traffic control network on Monday, Trump delivered a metaphor for a political method specifically designed to create instability rather than calm. [Trump said,] ‘We essentially want to blow it up,’” Collinson wrote. “If that’s his plan, the transition to the world of AI… will be rocky. This is a moment when anxious citizens need transparency, honesty and consistency from their government. So far that’s lacking, which is another kind of system failure.”

What the right is saying.
  • Many on the right argue the outages result from poor systems and old equipment.
  • Some suggest a bad actor is likely involved. 
  • Others say that a high-tech society has inherent vulnerabilities.

On his Substack, Erick-Woods Erickson said “I’d sleep better if it were the hackers.”

“If you know anything about the FAA, you should never presume hacking. Always presume incompetence and old equipment. This is an agency that still runs on floppy disks,” Erickson wrote. “The rest of it, I am convinced, is connected. Over the past couple of weeks, [several companies] announced they would be rolling out updates to keep AI agents from working inside their systems on behalf of consumers.”

“AI is finding holes in their systems faster than anyone expected, and they know that if their AI can find those holes, someone else’s AI can find them too,” Erickson said. “A cyberattack would at least mean someone, somewhere, was competent. What we actually have is critical infrastructure held together by old code and people scrambling to patch it before the real attacks come, and making a mess of it in the process. That is much harder to sleep through.”

In The American Spectator, Itxu Díaz argued “we need to know more.”

“One thing is becoming clear: we have entered an era of great uncertainty,” Díaz wrote. “I don’t believe, despite everything I’ve read on social media, that an out-of-control AI is causing all the world’s ills… I do believe AI is opening unexpected doors for the most dangerous hackers, who are not the ‘lone wolves’ but those working within the intelligence services of the world’s most dangerous nations, or those lurking in the back rooms of the most bloodthirsty terrorist groups.”

“We need answers, both from the major corporations affected and from governments. It is obvious that something has gone wrong in recent days, but it is not enough for the authorities simply to say that this is not a terrorist attack,” Díaz said. “I refuse to believe that no one is responsible for this string of disasters. It is one thing to reject conspiracy theories, but quite another to force us all to embrace Goofy-style thinking.”

In RedState, Ward Clark wrote about technology’s “fraying spots.” 

“Our modern, high-tech society is utterly dependent, now, on a vast, interconnected, technical system, run by software, increasingly managed by artificial intelligence (AI) and dependent on our vast and aging power grid and telecommunications network,” Clark said. “It’s inevitable that we will see glitches in the system from time to time, and some of those, as Secretary Rubio assures us, are not the work of malign actors or hackers. 

“Small disruptions can have large impact. The FAA’s technical problems caused a ground stop that had air travel around the nation tangled up for days. Outages at Apple and Microsoft could have easily caused big problems for business and personal accounts alike,” Clark wrote. “Related or not, what these incidents have revealed is that a small stone tossed into our collective online pool can cast some really outsized ripples. That’s something that’s worth bending a few brain cells to, and to prepare for.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • A few months ago, I was skeptical of AI warnings, but now I think they’re coming true.
  • Companies are rapidly trying to patch vulnerabilities in their systems and breaking things along the way.
  • I’m highly concerned about what that means for the durability of these systems going forward.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Back in April, Anthropic announced a new AI model called “Mythos” and said it was too dangerous to be released to the public. 

The company’s general message was: We built a product that’s so good at finding security vulnerabilities that we can’t release it publicly right now. Instead, we’ll launch a project (named Glasswing) to give American businesses a head start to shore up their security vulnerabilities before the public gets access to these tools. Anthropic said it expected other models to catch up in the coming months, at which point we’d see a slew of new tech vulnerabilities and cyber intrusions pop up across the world.

I saw this story through a simple lens: Anthropic was like a company selling a security system while telling you it had just identified all these fresh ways a burglar could break into your home. It was fear-mongering. Before, I’d been skeptical of these companies’ claims about their products; now, I was outright scornful. It felt like a marketing ploy from a bunch of people who were getting very good at talking about how powerful and advanced their product was.

I also wrote this:

If, over the next few months, everyone from Amazon to Chase to Meta starts scrambling to prepare for a new security threat, that will confirm to me that this threat is real. If these guys all play with the model and nothing really changes, I’ll assume that the threat was overhyped.

Well, it’s now been a few months. I pride myself on being an open-minded person willing to admit when I’m wrong and change my mind when presented with new evidence. Today, I have to admit: The threat is beginning to look very, very real. So it’s time for me to eat some crow and update my assessment. 

Based on our knowledge right now, the wave of outages, tech issues, and general all-encompassing tech fragility across various sectors is not the result of rogue AI bots. It isn’t cybercriminals, and it’s not Iran or China, either. It appears to be exactly what Anthropic said would happen. A bunch of large corporations, institutions, and tech companies are using rapidly developing AI tools to identify their own security issues. Then they are trying to update, patch, and fix those issues. And in many cases, they are breaking things along the way.

That’s really it. That’s the story: AI-assisted corporations and institutions are in a race against AI-assisted threats, and everyone is moving so fast that our already fragile systems are beginning to crack. 

It isn’t your imagination that this is happening more frequently, either. Yes, part of it is that we are just noticing these failures — and this tech fragility — more. But we are also actually experiencing a higher frequency of outages. Rohit Krishnan, a Wharton fellow and author of Building God: Demystifying AI for Decision Makers, put together a helpful chart mapping rates of tech outages from the last 10 years. It shows we are not at all-time highs, but we are in a period of much higher system failures than normal. According to Krishnan, we haven’t seen this volume of disruptions across sectors since 2013. 

All of this has me seriously reconsidering my rather blasé attitude about the rapid development of AI. Among other things, in recent writings, I’ve said that on a scale of 1 to 10, with 1 being the very early stages of AI capabilities and 10 being AI as a fully realized technology, I think we are closer to a 7 than a 3. In other words, these models weren’t going to get much better than they are now. 

That thesis is looking less likely every day. The models and products are continuing to improve rapidly, and we are not getting many signals that they are slowing down. Mythos was just one marker on the highway, but Anthropic's warnings about what models like it would do appear to be accurate. 

I’ve also been skeptical about how dangerous it would be to allow these products to hit the open market. But a collection of events has changed my opinion there, too: I’ve had several conversations with friends, readers, and experts in the space who convinced me I should be more worried than I am. I listened to Bill Gates’s recent interview with Ezra Klein, which genuinely scared me, not least because Gates himself seemed so thoroughly afraid. The Google Threat Intelligence Group then warned this week that the “era of autonomous attacks has arrived,” and we are now up against a “hacker that doesn’t eat, sleep, or get tired, and never stops searching for a way in.” And through all of this, I’ve been watching news story after news story about all the ways major industries seem unprepared for this moment. 

Think about it this way: The FAA called a national ground stop, the NSA had an internal communication system crash, and online banking service issues popped up all in just the last week. Each was (purportedly) caused by attempts to update or patch vulnerable systems. Which has me thinking: If the people trying to be helpful can so easily break the things they are working to improve, what does that say about the odds that actual AI-assisted cyber criminals (or, God forbid, rogue AI agents) will have much trouble bringing all these institutions to their knees?

Given all this, I feel much less confident about our potential to prevent a banking collapse, rogue AI from escaping containment, or government systems from being compromised. All of a sudden, a multi-week grid collapse or the potential for the U.S. military to be kneecapped in a “cyber incident” doesn’t seem so far-fetched. It’s honestly starting to feel a little Pollyannaish to think it won’t happen.

There’s no “but” here. I’m frustrated and a little uneasy to say that I don’t have an optimistic landing. I take solace in people like John Hultquist, the chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, who said this week, “Things are going to go offline periodically as the world manages a generation of tech debt. It will be a nuisance, but it will be okay.” I hope it’s as simple as that, but I can’t say I share his optimism anymore.

The people leading the AI revolution seem hellbent on pushing forward no matter the cost, despite their constant warnings that they might wipe out all of humanity. The government leaders responsible for regulating away the dangers of these kinds of technologies are busy obsessing over what we call them, or are totally in cahoots with the AI leaders themselves, or are so technically illiterate that any attempt to be helpful is nearly useless. And the rest of us common folk are just along for the ride.

So here’s to hoping the techies, nerds, and their billionaire bosses know what they’re doing. Because it’s starting to feel like the game is afoot. And I can’t say I’m keen to find out who wins.

Staff dissent.
Will Kaback
Senior Editor
 
Assuming that most of the recent disruptions are a byproduct of companies and government agencies trying to patch vulnerabilities identified by new AI models, I have a different reaction than Isaac.
 
He writes, “If the people trying to be helpful can so easily break the things they are working to improve, what does that say about the odds that actual AI-assisted cyber criminals (or, God forbid, rogue AI agents) will have much trouble bringing all these institutions to their knees?” I would be far more alarmed if this work wasn’t being done — that is, it’s relatively reassuring that new vulnerabilities are being found and urgent work is being done to address them. That things are breaking along the way isn’t ideal, obviously, but I think it’s a reasonable price to pay to improve critical systems. I don’t see it as evidence that we’re on the precipice of mass cyberattacks.
 
I appreciate Isaac’s message about keeping an open mind on new developments, and I want to do the same. If the disruptions and outages become more significant — a major bank going down for multiple days, issues with the electrical grid, another ground stop that persists for more than a few hours — I’ll start to see the trade-offs differently. Just today, the European Commission said it was targeted by an “AI-generated cybercampaign,” and that’s cause for real concern. Similarly, if AI-enabled cyberattacks become more frequent and impactful despite the work being done to prevent them, I think it will mean Isaac’s theory is, distressingly, coming true.
 
For now, though, I’m viewing the underlying work behind the recent system outages more optimistically.

Take the survey: Do you think outages will grow more disruptive to daily life? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The Senate considers permitting reform.
item.dc:creator: Will Kaback
item.description: Plus, a question about Samuel Alito and the Supreme Court.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The Senate permitting bill. On Monday, November 16, the Senate voted 70–27 to end debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a major permitting reform bill. The decision sets up a final Senate vote on the legislation, and if passed, it would then go to the House. The 494-page bill would constitute the most comprehensive permitting reform in decades, significantly overhauling existing processes for building projects that require federal approval. 

Back up: Federal permitting for building projects is primarily regulated by environmental protection statutes enacted throughout the 1960s and 70s. As time has passed, delays to major building projects — including clean-energy developments — have become more common, prompting calls for reforming the process. BAAJA comes after months of bipartisan negotiation in the Senate and was introduced by Democratic and Republican senators on the Environment and Public Works and Energy and Natural Resources committees.

BAAJA would significantly reform four existing statutes: the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), the Clean Water Act (CWA), and the Endangered Species Act (ESA). In each case, the bill would limit the existing law’s scope when it comes to reviewing and denying permits for new building projects; BAAJA’s changes attempt to preserve core environmental protections while removing more restrictive provisions. It additionally includes provisions that would hinder the executive branch’s ability to block permits; streamline the process for approving transmission lines; digitize the federal permitting process; and reform processes for hydropower, offshore energy, hardrock mining mill sites, and geothermal and nuclear energy projects.

On November 7, the bill’s sponsors released a manager’s amendment to the bill, giving Native American tribes greater determinative power in many of the suggested reformed processes; the amendment also clarified language in the bill’s permitting certainty section.

President Trump, energy developers and labor unions have expressed support for the bill; however, climate groups largely oppose it. Democrats are split, with some arguing lawmakers should delay action until Democrats assume large majorities in both chambers of Congress next year.

Below, you’ll hear views on the bill from the right and the left. Then, Senior Editor Will Kaback’s take.

What the right is saying.
  • The right supports the bill, with many expecting it to expedite projects.
  • Some argue BAAJA offers strong bipartisan solutions.
  • Others criticize climate activists for resisting permit reform.

The National Review editors called the bill “a golden opportunity for permitting reform.”

“Republican lawmakers have long sought to ease permitting for fossil-fuel production, while Democrats have wished to do the same only for clean energy. They joined for the rare congressional deal that improves matters in both directions,” the editors wrote. “If Republicans had drafted the legislation alone, they likely would have included more provisions from their 2023 legislation aimed at expanding oil and gas production.

“Yet compromise is a political necessity for any lasting reform effort, and to the extent the Senate has moved the ball forward on permitting, it has done so overwhelmingly toward deregulation and growth,” the editors said. “For once, Congress has taken initiative and done serious work to improve the nation’s laws… When they return from the midterm elections, lawmakers will have an elusive opportunity to clear roadblocks for infrastructure and energy projects of all sorts. They should seize it.”

In Cato at Liberty, Travis Fisher and Michael Abi-Nader said “America’s private sector is ready to build.”

“BAAJA builds on previous reform efforts, such as Manchin-Barrasso’s EPRA in 2024 and this term’s SPEED and PERMIT Acts,” Fisher and Abi-Nader wrote. “This moment is different for myriad reasons — electricity demand growth is reaching levels not seen this century, costly Biden-era energy subsidies have mostly been cut or curtailed, and Democrats now understand how much damage a president can inflict when he despises certain forms of energy.”

“And the stakes are high. Consulting firm McKinsey estimated in 2025 that up to $1.5 trillion in infrastructure investment was awaiting federal permits,” Fisher and Abi-Nader said. “BAAJA is an excellent set of bipartisan reforms. Not perfect by any means, but a substantial movement in the right direction. Our question to policymakers is this: Will you embrace reform, or will the federal government continue to deny permission for much-needed energy projects?”

In the Daily Caller, David Blackmon suggested the bill “would put [advocacy] groups out of the problem-creating business.”

“The Natural Resources Defense Council, the Sierra Club and a swarm of allied activist groups are trying to kill the most serious permitting reform bill Congress has taken up in years,” Blackmon wrote. “They oppose it because it would shrink the bureaucratic rot and litigation veto that keep them in business. It is no surprise these conflict groups oppose a bill which would help resolve conflicts. These groups exist to preserve and extend conflicts, not to solve them.”

“The conflict groups could not stop the first vote. They are now trying to peel Democrats off before final passage... and to park the bill until January. The country cannot afford that delay. American energy demand is rising in every part of the economy,” Blackmon said. “[The bill] would put real deadlines on reviews… limit the lawsuit treadmill used to stop projects, and require data centers to pay their own way. That is why the bill needs to become law.”

What the left is saying.
  • The left is mixed, with some saying the legislation removes important environmental protections.
  • Some celebrate the bill’s potential to enable future renewable energy projects.
  • Others express concern that BAAJA gives President Trump too much power.

In CounterPunch, Katie Bilodeau said BAAJA will “[remove] much of the remaining protective measures.”

“BAAJA is described as ‘permit reform,’ which simply means it amends environmental laws,” Bilodeau wrote. “This isn’t just about energy projects. The bill would amend environmental laws themselves, including any project proposed for public land or that uses a significant amount of taxpayer money. Think of logging projects, fish-poisoning projects, or roadbuilding projects as well as mining projects.”

“BAAJA presumes that all government decisions are good, so they should be hard to challenge and the decision should remain in force, even if laws were broken to get there,” Bilodeau said. “Bills are inherently value-driven. Proclaiming that S. 5653 ‘cuts red tape’ clarifies that the real driving value is to eliminate current environmental protections, which would allow our government to authorize environmental damage with little accountability.”

In The New York Times, Ezra Klein argued “leaving the system unchanged is a guarantee of calamity.”

“I don’t want this column to read as more confident about this bill than I really am… Legislation at this scale rarely plays out exactly as its architects expect,” Klein wrote. “But at its core, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would do the same thing over and over again: It would make it faster and simpler to build energy infrastructure by rolling back the opportunities for delays, lawsuits and vetoes that have proliferated in recent decades.”

“The problem, right now, is that we cannot meet enough new demand… with renewables. What the act might make possible is the construction of an energy grid where there is enough renewable power to meet new demand. In the absence of that energy system, new demand would be met by fossil fuels,” Klein said. “I don’t dismiss the concerns any [Democrats] have about this bill. But it’s a risk worth taking to make the future they’ve promised possible.”

In Common Dreams, Dean Baker suggested returning to permit reform “after Trump is gone and democracy is restored.”

“I have long been familiar with the argument for permitting reform and am largely in agreement,” Baker wrote. “But I still can’t buy Ezra Klein’s enthusiastic endorsement of the bill [in] the New York Times over the weekend. The point is that the bill will substantially reduce opportunities to block energy- and infrastructure-related projects. That is a great idea, but not with Donald Trump in the White House and picking the projects.”

“[Trump] has already said that he will deny permits to wind turbines, apparently due to a hatred resulting from their placement near one of his golf courses in Scotland. It’s a safe bet that Trump will do everything in his power, and then some, to block the development of clean energy in his last two years in office,” Baker said. “The framing of this as a short-term ‘affordability’ story, as Klein does, is Washington-silly.”

My take.
Will Kaback
Senior Editor
 
 
  • I’ve grown accustomed to legislative inaction, so a major bipartisan bill like this gives me some hope. 
  • Critics of BAAJA have valid concerns, but the bill’s trade-offs are worth it. 
  • Passing the bill may build sorely needed policymaking momentum in Congress.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Since I began writing for Tangle, I’ve spent many a take bemoaning legislative inaction as the executive and judicial branches assert more and more power. So today, I’m glad (excited, even) to be writing about a bill that’s not only ambitious and bipartisan, but has a strong chance of becoming law, too. Congress is doing something! Best of all, I think it’s doing something good.

Let’s start with the central premise of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA): Infrastructure permitting processes in the U.S. are too slow, expensive and fragmented, making it harder to meet energy needs and driving up prices for consumers. Consider a few examples of how difficult it has become to build energy projects in the United States. According to an Energy Department report, “The number of miles of newly built high-voltage transmission has declined… from an average of 2,500 miles each year from 2013–2015 to just 56 miles in 2023.” And 2021–2024 was the slowest four years of high-voltage transmission line construction since at least 2010. Berkeley Lab’s Queued Up report found that at the end of 2025, roughly 8,200 projects were actively seeking grid interconnection in the U.S. 

Meanwhile, the median time to complete the environmental impact statements mandated by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) was 2.8 years from January 2019 to December 2024 (somewhat humorously, that’s an improvement of five months compared to 2010–2018). And while NEPA was designed (in part) to compel federal agencies to consider the environmental impacts of their decisions, some experts have found that these requirements actually bog down renewable energy projects that environmental advocates champion.  

The horror stories caused by the current system are everywhere — a “fast-tracked” power project that was finally approved after 17 years, a wind farm project that was abandoned after 16 years, a natural gas pipeline that didn’t start operating for six years after construction began. It’s a mess, and as writers on the right and left agreed upon above, unwinding the tangle of environmental reviews, disparate agency requirements, and complex approval processes is imperative for the U.S. to meet rising energy demand (and keep costs in check). 

Hearteningly, both sides also agree on a key piece of that reform. The bill would empower the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to approve new interstate transmission lines when proposals hit snags at the state level, along with a slew of other provisions to expedite new builds and upgrade existing ones. As National Review’s editors noted (under “What the right is saying”), the reforms would also remove barriers to emerging energy sources like geothermal and hydropower, bolstering an all-of-the-above energy policy. 

I could spend the rest of this take writing about other provisions I like in BAAJA, like accelerating nuclear power adoption and protecting consumers from higher energy bills linked to new data center construction. But its limitations are just as important to discuss. 

Legal scholar Steve Vladeck made the strongest argument I’ve read against passing the bill in its current form. He highlights how BAAJA would remove or weaken key legal remedies for potential violations of environmental laws while making it harder for courts to review or undo federal agencies’ permitting decisions. It would restrict the president’s ability to block already-approved permits, but also empower them to prioritize their preferred projects. That puts enormous power in the president’s hands. 

Currently, that’s President Trump, who has two more years in office and is eager to sign BAAJA into law. His critics are sounding the alarm that the bill would allow him to spend his remaining time blocking clean energy projects (and greenlighting new fossil fuel development). The president has a tendency to rush certain projects on dubious legal grounds, and this law could further embolden him. Conversely, a hypothetical Democratic president in 2029 could spend the next four years sidelining new (and necessary) fossil fuel projects and boosting “green energy” in ways that enrage the right. You can see the dilemma for both sides. Are we really fixing the permitting system if we just open it up to presidential whiplash every four or eight years, creating new uncertainty for developers and eliminating legal pathways to constrain executive overreach?

Environmental concerns loom large over this debate. A bill that seeks to introduce efficiency and order to permitting processes sounds great on paper, but what if some of the “inefficiencies” existed for good reason? For instance, if a proposed project could create environmental hazards for a community or pollute a waterway or disrupt a local economy, maybe we shouldn’t be speeding through its approval process. A more methodical approach, while frustrating at times, offers a buffer against decisions that could harm people and the environment. 

Ultimately, these concerns don’t convince me to oppose the bill. Many of its critics suggest that it would destroy all meaningful environmental review and enable unchecked pollution — that isn’t the case. The bill changes NEPA, but it doesn’t eliminate it. Environmental impact statements are still required, agencies will still have to consider the environmental risks of proposals, and regulations are still in place to curb air and water pollution. The timelines for those processes will be accelerated and certain considerations removed, but projects will still face considerable scrutiny before winning approval. 

Even still, some of the concerns I flagged could be addressed by holding the bill through the lame-duck session and taking it back up with the Democratic Congress in the new year. But getting to this point took months of hard negotiations, and I think it’s far from guaranteed that Republicans would maintain their support if the bill stalled out now. Furthermore, the ultimate travesty would be allowing fear of what President Trump (or any future president) might do to scuttle reforms with so much potential. 

BAAJA’s trade-offs are worth it. Realizing a future of more robust, sustainable, and affordable energy projects involves taking risks, and this bill has plenty. But we have no shot at getting there with the status quo. 

Plus, don’t discount what passing BAAJA could do for our national psyche. As I wrote earlier, Congress’s inaction or indifference on so many issues has been maddening for all of my adult life. Obviously, they’ve passed some major bills in recent years, and one permitting reform bill isn’t exactly a sea change. But the legislative branch has become historically unproductive, and passing a bill like this would show that even a polarized Congress can still do things. It’d be a demonstration of competence and responsiveness at a time when it’s sorely needed. I hope lawmakers recognize this opportunity. 

Take the survey: What do you think of BAAJA? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: Jensen Huang’s resignation and Nvidia’s future.
item.dc:creator: Kmele Foster
item.description: The scandal could have far-reaching consequences.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia. On Thursday, technology company Nvidia announced CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation following reports that he had multiple extramarital relationships, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia has hired an outside firm to investigate the claims and has faced increasing scrutiny from public officials over its business practices. Separately, on Monday, the Justice Department and Commerce Department announced that investigations into the company associated with the alleged spy have been underway since 2024. 

Back up: Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and grew the company into a leading developer of computer chips used for gaming, data science, high-performance computing, artificial intelligence (AI), and more. It is one of the largest companies in the world by market capitalization, with Huang serving as a widely recognized voice on AI development. 

Huang is alleged to have had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese national and business executive who joined the Singaporean cloud computing company Megaspeed in 2023. The company then purchased billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and came under suspicion of illegally diverting those chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. In February, Singapore barred Alice Huang from entering the country for allegedly misrepresenting her role with Megaspeed, but the country did not prosecute her for any crime or investigate her for espionage. Megaspeed has denied breaking any laws and said that Huang left the company in 2025.

Alice Huang and Jensen Huang were first photographed together in December 2023 and have been seen together in public several times since. This spring, Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo to top Trump administration officials informing them that U.S. officials knew of a close relationship between the two, and that they believed Alice Huang had been recruited as a spy. President Donald Trump was also reportedly briefed on the intelligence findings in October 2025 but did not take action at the time.

In a November 8 email to Nvidia employees, Huang acknowledged having an affair and apologized to his family and colleagues, though he did not address his relationship with Alice Huang specifically. Three days later, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an extramarital affair with the company’s vice president of health care; the next day, Reuters reported that he had an intimate relationship with a different employee. Neither Nvidia nor Huang has commented on these additional allegations. 

President Trump and some tech leaders have expressed support for Huang in the wake of his resignation. On Monday, Trump said he “would not mind” if Huang were reinstated as CEO and rejected the suggestion that the relationship with Alice Huang risked U.S. national security. Separately, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has repeatedly criticized Nvidia, questioning the company’s culture and saying it requires a “dramatic shakeup” after Huang’s resignation. Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department is responsible for enforcing restrictions on certain AI chip exports to China, are traveling with President Trump to China this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders’ Meeting. Ahead of that trip, the administration issued an interim final rule closing a loophole that had allowed China to access advanced compute power by renting it from data centers outside the country. 

Today, we’ll have views from the left and right on the fallout from Huang’s resignation, followed by Editor-at-Large Kmele Foster’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • Many on the left criticize the leadership structure of top tech companies. 
  • Some question Commerce Secretary Lutnick’s decision making. 
  • Others say Jensen Huang’s successor faces a daunting task.

In The American Prospect, Ryan Cooper argued “this is the problem with oligarchy.”

“Huang is out because, remarkably enough, Nvidia is one of the better-governed tech companies,” Cooper wrote. “That said, Huang had still made himself the center of the business in many ways. He was a quintessential Silicon Valley hero-founder, always wearing his signature leather jacket, and treated like a celebrity around the world. He reportedly had 60 people reporting directly to him, as compared to the traditional five to seven for a CEO.”

“This mess leaves multiple large question marks hanging over global society… In addition to general chaos and market panic unleashed by this scandal, it may cause a sharp decline in Nvidia’s sales, if not huge legal sanctions for violating American law,” Cooper said. “What knock-on effects might that have on the financial companies that lent the money? That’s how a financial crisis gets rolling… Hyper-concentration of markets means that one man’s sexual indiscretions can become an entire planet’s economic problem.”

In Bloomberg, Jonathan Levin suggested “questions around [Lutnick]… keep growing.”

“[Howard Lutnick] has oversight of US export control programs and has to ensure that certain goods don’t fall into the hands of bad actors or anyone posing a threat to US national security. Yet, that’s exactly what Lutnick may have allowed to happen. And Congress now rightly wants answers,” Levin wrote. “The whole situation raises many troubling questions, starting with why Lutnick didn’t crack down on Nvidia chip exports to certain countries including Singapore.”

“He’s also failed to insulate himself from financial conflicts of interest. Cantor Fitzgerald, which is now run by Lutnick’s sons, has drawn attention for multiple conflicts given the firm’s intersection with the commerce secretary’s own wallet,” Levin said. “Lutnick is going to have to account for all of this, in what promises to be closely watched congressional hearings that will explore possible betrayals of national security in the interest of self-aggrandizement.”

In Semafor, Reed Albergotti said “Nvidia’s next CEO will have to keep an entire industry alive.”

“Nvidia got caught without a succession plan for CEO Jensen Huang, but it wasn’t for lack of trying, according to people briefed on the effort to hire a replacement,” Albergotti wrote. “Before the 63-year-old founder was ousted, the company did try to hire an external number two, according to a person familiar with the search. It was difficult to find candidates, though, because none wanted to work in Huang’s shadow.

“The Huang hangover might still be a problem even after he’s gone. There’s a Slack group at the company, for instance, titled ‘Stand with Jensen,’ and people familiar with the search process estimate there are fewer than 10 people in the world truly capable of running the company,” Albergotti said. “The next Nvidia CEO doesn’t just have to keep its own products shipping on time. The person who takes the top job also has to keep the entire industry alive. There’s really no replacing him.”

What the right is saying.
  • Many on the right suggest the saga will damage China’s AI development efforts.
  • Some call for investigations into the Trump administration.
  • Others suggest the scandal proves the U.S.’s AI dominance.

In The Spectator, Matthew Lynn suggested “China is the real loser from the Jensen Huang affair.”

“In the short term people may be impressed by the reach of [China’s] intelligence operations. It is no minor achievement to plant any agent right at the heart of one of the world’s most important companies. And yet, once all the headlines have blown over, it will have three longer-term consequences,” Lynn wrote. “Its spying operations have been sensationally exposed… China has been rumbled, and it will be trusted far less after this episode.”

“Next, it will be very hard to honeytrap any more CEOs… Finally, Nvidia will have to be a lot more careful from now on. Deals that might have been possible if the honeytrap operation had never happened will now be completely impossible,” Lynn said. “The mission has rebounded on its own authors. There is still a bitter contest between China and the United States to control the technology… China has just made it a lot harder for itself.”

In The Wall Street Journal, Peggy Noonan argued “Huang is a White House scandal.”

“It is important it not be misunderstood as a merely personal story, a private matter,” Noonan wrote. “It is a story about our national security, and it carries implications in all aspects of U.S. defense and cybersecurity. It is a story about an administration’s failure to take responsibility and stop harm, for reasons that are mysterious. And of course it is about a successful top-level espionage operation carried out against America by its foremost world challenger, China.”

“Mr. Trump was saying we have to beat China while his top AI adviser appears to have been helping China win the future,” Noonan said. “If the president knew about Mr. Huang’s situation and did nothing, that is a scandal. If U.S. intelligence figures alerted the Commerce Department there was a problem with a Chinese spy and cutout companies, and Commerce did nothing, that is a scandal… There should be public hearings and investigations to drill down to the bottom of this story and get to the truth.”

In the Daily Signal, Randy Forbes said the scandal proves “why we need American tech companies.”

“[Huang’s resignation is] the latest reminder of Beijing’s determination to get its hands on American technology,” Forbes wrote. “Much has been made about the artificial intelligence race between the U.S. and China, but less is said about the semiconductor components that go into AI. It’s estimated that 65% of China’s AI capacity will come from U.S. semiconductors by the end of next year. This is how significant the American advantage is.”

“In spite of endless Chinese IP theft and state subsidies, the U.S. remains ahead in both AI models and AI computing components. Why? In 2025, the United States had 1,953 newly funded AI companies compared with just 161 in China. This was driven by $286 billion in private AI investment, compared with a mere $12.4 billion in China,” Forbes said. “If we want to truly beat China on chips, AI, and other tech, then we know the way forward. The U.S. should make it even easier for new entrants into the tech sector.”

My take.
Kmele Foster
Editor-at-Large
 
 
  • While I maintain sympathy for Jensen Huang, his actions deserve serious scrutiny.
  • Key details of this story are still evolving, but based on what we know, Huang’s affair will have cascading consequences.
  • The biggest consequence could be losing a leading advocate for technological progress.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

I was singing bedtime songs with my kids last night when I realized I’d need to rework the take you’re reading now.

I’ve spent the past several days poring over scores of media reports and commentary about Jensen Huang’s resignation. The controversy surrounding his departure from one of the world’s most valuable companies is startling, all too familiar, and, at the same time, surprisingly unresolved. Originally, I wanted to write a biting rebuke of Jensen and his decision making. But as I sat with my kids last night, I felt a pang of sympathy for him. His children are grown — in fact, they work for the company he co-founded — but I imagined them together at bedtime years ago. And I imagined the shame I’d feel if my own children, at any age, were reading disreputable revelations about me in the press.

Like all of us, I’ve said and done things that hurt the people I care about. I’ve disappointed those closest to me. And for a period, during a particularly dark stretch, those weren’t isolated lapses. I’m grateful to have had the chance to make amends and grow from those experiences. And I’m especially grateful never to have made the sort of relationship-altering choices Jensen has now admitted to. 

But Jensen isn’t an ordinary civilian enduring some private embarrassment. He had been Nvidia’s chief executive since co-founding the company more than thirty years ago, and his foresight helped position the company to achieve unparalleled technological and commercial heights. In October, the company’s market valuation approached $6 trillion, nearly a trillion dollars more than Apple. But by the beginning of this month, The New York Times was publishing deeply reported pieces on Jensen’s affair with an alleged spy. Jensen’s resignation followed soon after, indirectly acknowledging his marital infidelity but saying nothing specific about which of his extramarital relationships he was apologizing for. 

Ultimately, Jensen is responsible for his misconduct. His actions merit serious sanction for failing in his obligations to shareholders, breaching the board’s trust, and misleading the colleagues to whom he initially denied reports of his affairs. And he’s responsible for any securities violations those failures might have caused.

Still, as I mentioned earlier, our understanding of this story is still evolving. Initial reporting presented Alice Huang as a Chinese Communist Party operative and Jensen as the target of a clandestine honeypot operation, though subsequent reporting on the intelligence community’s assessments has complicated that picture. If those allegations prove true, though, this is a major scandal with major national security implications, and reports that President Trump was briefed on the matter but failed to take serious action would describe a staggering dereliction of duty. If they don’t, the injustice of Alice Huang being framed as a foreign operative deserves acknowledgment, too.

In the meantime, tech executives, investors, and one president of the United States have publicly lobbied Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen as CEO, citing his unique abilities as a business leader, his singular importance to the development of artificial intelligence, and the imperative to maintain American dominance in the industry. An open letter signed by Nvidia employees and shareholders stresses the importance of due diligence when adjudicating allegations of corporate misconduct, warns against a rush to judgment, and notes the uncertainty surrounding some of the allegations about Alice Huang.

They’re right that much remains uncertain. But what’s clear to me is that Jensen has forfeited two of his most valuable assets: trust and credibility. 

Calls for due diligence are reasonable, but they aren’t an argument against accountability. A board’s first obligation is to the shareholders it serves, and a company’s culture is essential to keeping that relationship stable. Jensen misled the board that would be rehiring him, along with the colleagues and reporters who asked him directly about his actions. Returning him to the job without severe sanctions would tell every employee at Nvidia, and every executive watching from elsewhere, that candor with your board is optional if you’re valuable enough.

I’m also less convinced than his staunchest defenders that Jensen is indispensable. He’s an exceptional executive, and few people in American business have built more consequential products. But companies of Nvidia’s scale aren’t the work of one man, however gifted, and the engineers, researchers, and managers who built its products are still there. Apple survived the loss of Steve Jobs; Nvidia can survive the loss of Jensen Huang. Insisting otherwise badly underrates everyone else who made the company what it is (and will continue to be).

For my part, I suspect the most substantial loss here has a less direct relationship with Nvidia’s share price. Jensen is among the most persuasive public advocates for the idea that technological progress is worth wanting, not merely as a weapon in some contest with China, but as an engine of human flourishing. His pitch wasn’t always mine, but few people made the optimistic case with more authority. But that authority depends on credibility, and credibility is exactly what he’s exhausted. Whatever the board decides, Jensen can’t recover the thing that made him most valuable to determined techno-optimists like me. And his exit comes just as the doomers, cynics, and skeptics are ascendant and as a newly elected Congress decides what to do about AI and data centers. The case for progress still deserves to be made. I’m just less sure, this morning, who will make it.

Staff concurrence.
Will Kaback
Senior Editor
 
I think the Trump administration’s role in this story deserves comparable scrutiny to Jensen Huang’s and Nvidia’s. As Kmele notes, key details are still unconfirmed (including whether Alice Huang is actually a Chinese asset), but our current understanding raises serious questions about the administration’s decisions.
 
I’ve been most attuned to the growing rift between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. In Bessent’s telling, his department (and Defense, State, and the U.S. trade representative) long supported putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist over concerns it was helping China illegally access Nvidia chips, but Lutnick resisted the idea. Bessent has now spent the past week publicly haranguing the Commerce Department, and I expect scrutiny of Lutnick’s decisions to intensify — and rightfully so.
 
The New York Times has reported on clear conflicts of interest between Lutnick’s role as Commerce secretary and the business activities of his sons at their firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, which stood to benefit from a laxer approach to AI chip export controls. Even setting aside those potential conflicts, the public deserves answers on Lutnick’s reluctance to crack down on Megaspeed.
 
Separately, I agree with Kmele that President Trump’s inaction when briefed on Alice Huang and Megaspeed over one year ago represents a “staggering dereliction of duty” if confirmed. How differently would this story have played out if the administration had simply notified Nvidia of its suspicions about Alice Huang after the president was briefed? How much did the administration know about Megaspeed allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China? Why is the president still expressing support for Huang and even suggesting he should be reinstated as CEO?
 
As stunning as this story already is, we still have much to learn. I hope Congress can do its part to help find answers.
